worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1-3{e}^{4t}} & =L{1}+L{-3{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{1}-3L{{e}^{4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

$$
L{1}=\frac{1}{s},\,s>0
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{1}-3L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{s}-3\cdot \frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{1}{s}-\frac{3}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-3s}{s(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{2(s+2)}{s(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{1}$ is defined for $s\in (0,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(0,\infty )\cap (4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$
